2|ARCHES: A Randomized, Phase III Study of
3|Androgen Deprivation Therapy With
4|Enzalutamide or Placebo in Men With Metastatic
5|Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer
6|Andrew J. Armstrong, MD, ScM1; Russell Z. Szmulewitz, MD2; Daniel P. Petrylak, MD3; Jeffrey Holzbeierlein, MD4; Arnauld Villers, MD5;
7|Arun Azad, MBBS, PhD6; Antonio Alcaraz, MD, PhD7; Boris Alekseev, MD8; Taro Iguchi, MD, PhD9; Neal D. Shore, MD10;
8|Brad Rosbrook, MS11; Jennifer Sugg, MS12; Benoit Baron, MS13; Lucy Chen, MD12; and Arnulf Stenzl, MD14
9|abstract
10|PURPOSE Enzalutamide, a potent androgen-receptor inhibitor, has demonstrated significant benefits in met-
11|astatic and nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. We evaluated the efficacy and safety of
12|enzalutamide in metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC).
13|METHODS ARCHES (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02677896) is a multinational, double-blind, phase III trial,
14|wherein 1,150 men with mHSPC were randomly assigned 1:1 to enzalutamide (160 mg/day) or placebo, plus
15|androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), stratified by disease volume and prior docetaxel chemotherapy. The
16|primary end point was radiographic progression-free survival.
17|RESULTS As of October 14, 2018, the risk of radiographic progression or death was significantly reduced with
18|enzalutamide plus ADT versus placebo plus ADT (hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.30 to 0.50; P , .001; median
19|not reached v 19.0 months). Similar significant improvements in radiographic progression-free survival were
20|reported in prespecified subgroups on the basis of disease volume and prior docetaxel therapy. Enzalutamide
21|plus ADT significantly reduced the risk of prostate-specific antigen progression, initiation of new antineoplastic
22|therapy, first symptomatic skeletal event, castration resistance, and reduced risk of pain progression. More men
23|achieved an undetectable prostate-specific antigen level and/or an objective response with enzalutamide plus
24|ADT (P , .001). Patients in both treatment groups reported a high baseline level of quality of life, which was
25|maintained over time. Grade 3 or greater adverse events were reported in 24.3% of patients who received
26|enzalutamide plus ADT versus 25.6% of patients who received placebo plus ADT, with no unexpected adverse
27|events.
28|CONCLUSION Enzalutamide with ADT significantly reduced the risk of metastatic progression or death over time
29|versus placebo plus ADT in men with mHSPC, including those with low-volume disease and/or prior docetaxel,
30|with a safety analysis that seems consistent with the safety profile of enzalutamide in previous clinical trials in
31|castration-resistant prostate cancer.
32|J Clin Oncol 37:2974-2986. © 2019 by American Society of Clinical Oncology
33|Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives 4.0 License
34|INTRODUCTION
35|Globally, prostate cancer was the most common
36|cancer for men, with 1.4 million patients in 2016;
37|mortality was 381,000.1 In the United States, 174,650
38|new cases of prostate cancer are expected in 2019,
39|with 31,620 anticipated deaths.2 The majority of
40|deaths from prostate cancer are due to metastatic
41|disease, identified either at diagnosis or after relapse
42|following local therapies.3
43|Metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC),
44|defined as patients with metastatic disease who have
45|not yet received, or are continuing to respond to,
46|hormone therapy, accounts for up to 5% of annual
47|prostate cancer incidence in the United States.4 An-
48|drogen deprivation therapy (ADT) with a luteinizing
49|hormone-releasing hormone agonist/receptor antag-
50|onist or bilateral orchiectomy has been the standard of
51|care (SOC) for men with mHSPC.5 However, the
52|majority of men with mHSPC who receive ADT alone
53|progress to castration-resistant disease within 1 to
54|3 years, despite experiencing an initial response.5-7
55|Previous trials in men with mHSPC combining ADT with
56|other treatments such as docetaxel chemotherapy6,8
57|or the selective androgen biosynthesis inhibitor abir-
58|aterone acetate,9-11 hereafter referred to as abiraterone,

1|have demonstrated significant clinical benefits, including
2|significantly improved overall survival (OS), and these
3|combinations are now included in treatment guidelines as
4|part of the SOC.12,13 Abiraterone plus ADT is approved in
5|combination with prednisone for men with metastatic
6|high-risk castration-sensitive prostate cancer,14,15 on the
7|basis of the LATITUDE trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier:
8|NCT01715285),10 which exclusively enrolled men with
9|high-risk mHSPC and excluded previous chemotherapy.
10|The efficacy and safety of enzalutamide, a potent
11|androgen-receptor (AR) inhibitor,16 has been demon-
12|strated across the spectrum of castration-resistant
13|prostate cancer (CRPC) by numerous, large-scale,
14|randomized, controlled clinical trials.17-21 In addition,
15|a phase II, open-label, single-arm study investigating
16|enzalutamide monotherapy in patients with hormone-
17|na ̈ıve
18|prostate
19|cancer
20|demonstrated
21|long-term
22|re-
23|ductions in prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, with
24|minimal changes in overall bone mineral density and
25|global health status.22-24
26|Two recent studies that investigated abiraterone in addition
27|to ADT excluded men with prior docetaxel chemotherapy
28|and did not include prospective evaluation of results by
29|disease volume (high v low).10,11 ARCHES (Clinical-
30|Trials.gov identifier: NCT02677896) aimed to assess
31|efficacy and safety of enzalutamide plus ADT in men with
32|mHSPC, regardless of prior docetaxel or disease volume.
33|We hypothesized that enzalutamide, in combination with
34|ADT, would prolong radiographic progression-free sur-
35|vival (rPFS) in men with mHSPC, compared with
36|ADT alone.
37|METHODS
38|Study Design and Conduct
39|ARCHES is a multinational, double-blind, randomized,
40|placebo-controlled, phase III trial. The study protocol was
41|approved by local independent review boards and con-
42|ducted according to provisions of the Declaration of
43|Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice Guidelines of the
44|International Conference on Harmonisation. All patients
45|provided written informed consent. An independent Data
46|Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) evaluated unblinded
47|safety data on an ongoing basis. Please refer to the Dis-
48|closures for full information on data sharing.
49|Patients and Treatments
50|Eligible patients were adult (defined according to local
51|regulation) males with pathologically confirmed prostate
52|adenocarcinoma, without neuroendocrine differentiation,
53|signet-cell, or small-cell features, and an Eastern Co-
54|operative Oncology Group performance status score of 0 or
55|1. Eligible patients had hormone-sensitive metastatic dis-
56|ease, either de novo or after recurrence after prior local
57|therapy, documented by a positive bone scan, or metastatic
58|lesions on computed tomography or magnetic resonance
59|imaging. Enrollment was based on investigator-assessed
60|metastases; after study entry, metastasis was evaluated by
61|independent central review. Prior ADT and up to six cycles
62|of prior docetaxel chemotherapy were permitted. Patients
63|who experienced disease progression prior to randomiza-
64|tion while receiving ADT and/or docetaxel were excluded.
65|Additional details regarding inclusion/exclusion criteria are
66|provided in the Data Supplement.
67|Patients were centrally randomized 1:1 to enzalutamide
68|(160 mg/day) plus ADT or placebo plus ADT, stratified by
69|disease volume (low v high) and prior docetaxel chemo-
70|therapy for prostate cancer (no cycles, one to five cycles, or
71|six cycles). High-volume disease was defined as presence
72|of metastases involving the viscera, or in the absence of
73|visceral lesions, four or more bone lesions, one or more of
74|which must have been in a bony structure beyond the
75|vertebral column and pelvic bone, per CHAARTED (Clin-
76|icalTrials.gov identifier: NCT00309985) criteria.6 Treat-
77|ment continued until occurrence of unacceptable toxicity,
78|radiographic progression (confirmed by independent cen-
79|tral review), or initiation of an investigational agent or
80|new prostate cancer therapy. Subsequent therapy after
81|treatment discontinuation was permitted per local practice.
82|On the basis of the primary analysis results and DSMB
83|recommendation of study continuation, eligible patients
84|were offered the opportunity to transition to an open-label
85|extension.
86|End Points
87|The primary end point was rPFS, defined as the time from
88|randomization to the first objective evidence of radiographic
89|disease progression, as assessed by independent central
90|review or death (defined as death from any cause within
91|24 weeks from study drug discontinuation), whichever
92|occurred first. The cutoff of 24 weeks from study drug
93|discontinuation (ie, the second long-term follow-up visit) for
94|deaths (in the absence of disease progression) ensured
95|a similar follow-up period as for monitoring of radiographic
96|progression (ie, two 12-week radiologic assessment cycles
97|post-treatment discontinuation). In addition, sensitivity
98|analyses for rPFS were performed, including all deaths (in
99|the absence of evidence of radiographic progression) re-
100|gardless of timing, and radiographic progression docu-
101|mented by central review according to Prostate Cancer
102|Working Group 2 criteria,25 to assess the robustness of the
103|primary analysis; additional details are provided in Data
104|Supplement Table A1. Key secondary end points were time
105|to PSA progression, time to initiation of new antineoplastic
106|therapy (including cytotoxic and hormone therapies), PSA
107|undetectable rate, objective response rate, time to de-
108|terioration in urinary symptoms, and OS. Other secondary
109|end points included time to first symptomatic skeletal
110|event, time to castration resistance, patient-reported out-
111|comes (PROs), time to deterioration of quality of life (QoL),
112|and time to pain progression. Additional prespecified an-
113|alyses, per a separate PRO statistical analysis plan (SAP),

1|included QoL over time and sensitivity analyses of time
2|to pain progression (using other clinically meaningful
3|threshold criteria). Safety was also assessed. End point
4|definitions are provided in Data Supplement Table A1.
5|Assessments
6|Efficacy assessments included sequential radiographic
7|imaging performed at screening, at week 13, and every
8|subsequent 12 weeks. Radiographic progression events
9|were confirmed by independent central review; details
10|regarding the definition of radiographic progression, in-
11|cluding confirmatory scans required for new bone lesions
12|observed over time, are provided in Data Supplement
13|Table A2. PSA levels were measured at screening, at weeks
14|1, 5, and 13, every subsequent 12 weeks, and 30 days after
15|the last dose or prior to initiation of new antineoplastic
16|therapy for prostate cancer, whichever occurred first. PRO
17|assessments, such as Functional Assessment of Cancer
18|Therapy-Prostate,26 Quality of Life Prostate-Specific
19|questionnaire 25,27 and Brief Pain Inventory-Short
20|Form (BPI-SF), were completed at baseline, week 13,
21|and every 12 weeks thereafter. Adverse events (AEs) were
22|graded by the investigator according to the National
23|Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Ad-
24|verse Events (version 4.03).
25|Statistical Analysis
26|The final rPFS analysis was planned to occur after
27|262 events, to detect a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.67 with 90%
28|power, on the basis of a two-sided log-rank test and 5%
29|significance level. To adjust for multiplicity, a parallel testing
30|strategy was applied to the key secondary end points
31|(Appendix Fig A1, online only). Key secondary end
32|points, other than OS, were sequentially tested at a 1%
33|significance level. A final OS analysis will be performed
34|when 342 deaths have occurred to provide 80% power to
35|detect an HR of 0.73 at a 4% significance level. An interim
36|OS analysis was performed at the time of the final rPFS
37|analysis at a significance level calculated using the O'Brien-
38|Fleming function to control the overall alpha. Additional
39|details regarding the statistical analyses (original and final)
40|are provided in the Data Supplement (Fig A1 and Table A1)
41|and Protocol (including SAP).
42|RESULTS
43|Patients and Treatment
44|From March 21, 2016, to January 12, 2018, a total of 1,150
45|patients were randomly assigned 1:1 from 202 centers in
46|North and Latin America, Europe, and Asia; 1,146 patients
47|received at least one dose of the study drug (Fig 1).
48|Baseline demographics were well balanced between
49|treatment groups (Table 1); 727 patients (63.2%) had high-
50|volume disease, and 205 (17.9%) received prior docetaxel
51|chemotherapy. Use of concomitant antiandrogens as
52|prostate cancer therapy during the study was reported by
53|34 patients (5.9%) in the enzalutamide plus ADT group and
54|43 patients (7.5%) in the placebo plus ADT group.
55|As of the data cutoff on October 14, 2018, median follow-up
56|time was 14.4 months. Overall, 377 patients (32.8%) dis-
57|continued study treatment (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 135
58|[23.5%]; placebo plus ADT, n = 242 [42.0%]). The primary
59|reason for treatment discontinuation was progressive dis-
60|ease (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 65 [11.3%] v placebo plus
61|ADT, n = 171 [29.7%]), followed by patient withdrawal
62|(n = 25 [4.4%] v n = 30 [5.2%], respectively; Fig 1).
63|rPFS
64|At data cutoff, 292 radiographic disease progression events
65|or deaths without radiographic disease progression within
66|24 weeks of treatment discontinuation had occurred
67|(enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 91 [15.9%]; placebo plus
68|ADT, n = 201 [34.9%]; Table 2). Overall, enzalutamide plus
69|ADT significantly reduced the risk of radiographic disease
70|progression or death compared with placebo plus ADT by
71|61% (HR, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.30 to 0.50; P , .001; Fig 2A).
72|Median rPFS was not reached (NR) with enzalutamide plus
73|ADT (95% CI, NR to NR) versus 19.0 months (95% CI, 16.6
74|to 22.2 months) with placebo plus ADT. The treatment
75|effect of enzalutamide plus ADT was consistent across all
76|prespecified subgroups, including disease volume and
77|prior docetaxel chemotherapy (Fig 2B). A sensitivity
78|analysis of rPFS, including all deaths (in the absence of
79|evidence of radiographic disease progression) regardless of
80|timing, and a sensitivity analysis of radiographic progres-
81|sion documented by central review according to Prostate
82|Cancer Working Group 2 criteria25 were both consistent
83|with the primary analysis (Table 2).
84|Secondary End Points
85|The superiority of enzalutamide plus ADT over placebo plus
86|ADT was shown for the key secondary end points of time to
87|PSA progression, time to initiation of new antineoplastic
88|therapy, PSA undetectable rate, and objective response
89|rate (Table 2; Fig 3). Although the median time to initiation
90|of a new antineoplastic agent of 30.2 months in the
91|enzalutamide arm is not a reliable estimate because it
92|resulted from an event observed in the only remaining
93|patient at risk, the treatment effect was robust, as evi-
94|denced by the HR of 0.28 (95% CI, 0.20 to 0.40; P , .001).
95|Of the patients who initiated new antineoplastic therapy, the
96|most common therapy was abiraterone (n = 13; 28.3%)
97|followed by docetaxel (n = 11; 23.9%) in the enzalutamide
98|plus ADT group and docetaxel (n = 52; 39.1%) followed by
99|abiraterone and enzalutamide (n = 28 each; 21.1%) in the
100|placebo plus ADT group (Data Supplement Table A3). At
101|this interim OS analysis, data were immature, with
102|84 deaths (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 39; placebo plus ADT,
103|n = 45); median duration of OS was NR in either treatment
104|group (HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.53 to 1.25; P = .3361; Table 2;
105|Data Supplement Fig A2). Enzalutamide plus ADT also
106|significantly reduced the risk of a first symptomatic skeletal

4|total score, as a global indicator of QoL, was high at baseline

1|consideration of enzalutamide in addition to ADT for men
2|with mHSPC, including patients with prior docetaxel
3|treatment and regardless of disease volume. Although OS
4|data remain immature, these findings have clear clinical
5|implications for the current management of these patients.
6|PROs from assessments of daily living have also been
7|shown to predict survival in prostate cancer.29 In this
8|population of men with mHSPC, we observed maintenance
9|of high QoL over time, similar to that observed in the pop-
10|ulation with nonmetastatic castration-resistant disease.30
11|Baseline average BPI-SF scores were low overall, with
12|almost half of patients reporting scores of zero. Conse-
13|quently, no significant difference between treatment
14|groups in risk of pain progression, defined as a 30% or
15|greater increase in average BPI-SF pain severity score,
16|was observed. However, when using a more clinically
17|meaningful definition of pain progression ($ 2-point
18|threshold)31 during the prespecified sensitivity analyses
19|from the PRO SAP, enzalutamide plus ADT showed
20|a delay in pain progression versus placebo plus ADT.
21|Ultimately, no significant difference between treatment
22|groups in risk of deterioration of urinary symptoms or QoL
23|was observed, suggesting there was no negative impact on
24|PROs due to the addition of enzalutamide to ADT. Ad-
25|ditional analyses of the PROs are ongoing and are also
26|planned as part of the long-term follow-up.
27|Currently, ARCHES is the first trial to demonstrate clinically
28|meaningful benefits of potent AR inhibition with a second-
29|generation nonsteroidal antiandrogen (enzalutamide) in
30|combination with ADT, including a subgroup of men with
31|mHSPC after docetaxel chemotherapy. Whereas some pre-
32|vious studies focused on patients with high risk and entirely
33|excluded patients with previous chemotherapy,6-8,10,11 the
34|specific inclusion of patients with prior docetaxel chemo-
35|therapy in ARCHES provides unique insight into this im-
36|portant patient subgroup with unmet clinical needs.
37|Both rPFS and metastasis-free survival are accepted by the
38|US Food and Drug Administration as primary efficacy end
39|points in metastatic CRPC and nonmetastatic CRPC,
40|respectively.32,33 However, although rPFS has not yet been
41|established as a surrogate for OS in mHSPC, it is an ac-
42|ceptable regulatory end point, and reducing the risk of
43|radiographic progression or death is of clinical importance,
44|given the strong positive correlation reported for rPFS and
45|OS in patients with metastatic CRPC34,35 and the direct
46|impact of additional metastatic progression in this setting
47|on patient management. Furthermore, rPFS requires
48|shorter follow-up periods and fewer patients compared with
49|OS as a result of the higher event rate, accelerating trial
50|completion.36 It is also in the interest of patients to unblind
51|trials earlier, on the basis of robust rPFS evidence, espe-
52|cially when supported by strong secondary end points, to
53|allow crossover to active treatment. Therefore, ARCHES
54|was accelerated, with rPFS analysis conducted after only
55|262 events, despite an immature OS analysis. At the time of
56|manuscript submission, a phase III study investigating the
57|addition of enzalutamide versus a first-generation non-
58|steroidal antiandrogen, such as bicalutamide, to ADT, with
59|or without docetaxel chemotherapy, in men with mHSPC37
60|is currently ongoing and will provide additional data on the
61|clinical benefits of enzalutamide plus ADT, including the
62|impact on OS.
63|Several therapies have recently been shown to be effective in
64|men with mHSPC; therefore, ADT alone may no longer be an
65|appropriate control arm in this patient population. However,
66|docetaxel plus ADT only became part of the global SOC for
67|mHSPC in 2016, after patients were already enrolling in
68|ARCHES,12 and thus, docetaxel could not have been con-
69|sidered as part of the comparator arm in the current study.
70|Furthermore, patients with high-volume disease who had
71|completed prior docetaxel were eligible for trial entry by
72|study design, and for those with low-volume disease,
73|the benefit of early treatment with docetaxel combined
74|with ADT has not been established.13,38,39
75|In conclusion, in comparison with placebo, the addition of
76|enzalutamide to ADT for men with mHSPC provided clin-
77|ically meaningful improvements across key efficacy end
78|points while maintaining the high level of QoL reported at
79|baseline. Enzalutamide was generally well tolerated, with
80|a preliminary safety analysis seeming to be consistent with
81|the safety profile of enzalutamide in previous clinical trials
82|in CRPC. Enzalutamide plus ADT should therefore be
83|considered as a treatment option for men with mHSPC,
84|including those with low-volume disease or who had re-
85|ceived prior docetaxel. Additional studies are necessary to
86|clarify whether combination or sequential approaches with
87|AR-targeted therapies or chemotherapy are favored for
88|initial management.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

Sequence generation asks how the allocation sequence was produced; concealment asks whether forthcoming assignments were hidden before enrolment and assignment; baseline imbalance asks whether the resulting groups suggest a randomization problem. Evidence for one does not answer the others.
The baseline-imbalance answer must not change this answer.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the sequence method. A truncated search does not establish that the method is absent.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned to interventions?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if the trial used any form of remote or centrally administered method to allocate interventions to participants, where the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit or organization, independent of the enrolment personnel. Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. Answer ‘No’ if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.2
questions.bias_construct: Whether the allocation sequence was concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes for remote or centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel, or appropriately used opaque sequentially numbered sealed envelopes or identical sequentially numbered drug containers. Answer no when the enrolling investigator or participant could know the forthcoming allocation.
evidence_needed: The method used before assignment and who controlled it; for envelopes or containers, capture the details that make them tamper-resistant and irreversible before assignment.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the report does not provide enough information to assess concealment; do not infer concealment from central registration or a sequence number alone.

answer_anchors.text: Remote or central allocation was controlled by an independent external unit, or appropriate envelopes/containers were used.
The enrolling investigator or participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

considerations: Allocation concealment concerns the process before assignment, not blinding after assignment.

Keep concealment separate from sequence generation (how the sequence was made) and baseline imbalance (what the randomized groups look like). A random sequence or balanced baseline table does not establish concealment.
The reported sequence-generation method does not establish concealment.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the allocation safeguards. A truncated search does not establish that concealment details are absent.

questions.wording: Did baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with the randomization process?
questions.official_guidance: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.

questions.bias_construct: Whether baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with randomization.
questions.decision_rule: Answer no when no imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance. Answer yes for substantial group-size differences, an excess of statistically significant baseline differences beyond chance, a key prognostic imbalance very unlikely due to chance and large enough to bias the estimate, or excessive similarity incompatible with chance.
evidence_needed: Baseline characteristics for the randomized groups, intended allocation ratio, prognostic factors, and outcome baseline measures.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when no useful baseline information is available, for example in an abstract or when only final-analysis participants are described.

No imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance.

considerations: A few statistically significant differences at the conventional 0.05 threshold are usually compatible with chance.

Table A1. End Point Definitions and Analysis Method.
End point variable
Definition and analysis method
Primary
rPFS
Time from randomization to the first objective evidence
of radiographic disease progression as assessed by
central review or death (defined as death from any
cause within 24 weeks from study drug
discontinuation), whichever occurs first
Patients who discontinued study treatment without
confirmed radiographic progression continued the
radiographic assessment schedule until radiographic
progression was confirmed or the number of
radiographic progression events for the final rPFS
analysis was reached
Radiographic disease progression is defined as
progressive disease by RECIST, version 1.1,2 for soft
tissue disease or by appearance of two or more new
lesions on bone scan (see Supplementary Table S2)
Efficacy analyses were conducted on the intent-to-treat
population, defined as all randomized patients
A two-sided stratified log-rank test at a level of
significance of 0.05 was used to compare rPFS between

included QoL over time and sensitivity analyses of time
to pain progression (using other clinically meaningful
threshold criteria). Safety was also assessed. End point
definitions are provided in Data Supplement Table A1.
Assessments
Efficacy assessments included sequential radiographic
imaging performed at screening, at week 13, and every
subsequent 12 weeks. Radiographic progression events
were confirmed by independent central review; details
regarding the definition of radiographic progression, in-
cluding confirmatory scans required for new bone lesions
observed over time, are provided in Data Supplement
Table A2. PSA levels were measured at screening, at weeks
1, 5, and 13, every subsequent 12 weeks, and 30 days after
the last dose or prior to initiation of new antineoplastic
therapy for prostate cancer, whichever occurred first. PRO
assessments, such as Functional Assessment of Cancer
Therapy-Prostate,26 Quality of Life Prostate-Specific
questionnaire 25,27 and Brief Pain Inventory-Short
Form (BPI-SF), were completed at baseline, week 13,
and every 12 weeks thereafter. Adverse events (AEs) were
graded by the investigator according to the National
Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Ad-
verse Events (version 4.03).
Statistical Analysis
The final rPFS analysis was planned to occur after
262 events, to detect a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.67 with 90%
power, on the basis of a two-sided log-rank test and 5%
significance level. To adjust for multiplicity, a parallel testing
strategy was applied to the key secondary end points
(Appendix Fig A1, online only). Key secondary end
points, other than OS, were sequentially tested at a 1%
significance level. A final OS analysis will be performed
when 342 deaths have occurred to provide 80% power to
detect an HR of 0.73 at a 4% significance level. An interim
OS analysis was performed at the time of the final rPFS
analysis at a significance level calculated using the O'Brien-
Fleming function to control the overall alpha. Additional
details regarding the statistical analyses (original and final)
are provided in the Data Supplement (Fig A1 and Table A1)
and Protocol (including SAP).
RESULTS
Patients and Treatment
From March 21, 2016, to January 12, 2018, a total of 1,150
patients were randomly assigned 1:1 from 202 centers in
North and Latin America, Europe, and Asia; 1,146 patients
received at least one dose of the study drug (Fig 1).
Baseline demographics were well balanced between
treatment groups (Table 1); 727 patients (63.2%) had high-
volume disease, and 205 (17.9%) received prior docetaxel
chemotherapy. Use of concomitant antiandrogens as
prostate cancer therapy during the study was reported by
34 patients (5.9%) in the enzalutamide plus ADT group and
43 patients (7.5%) in the placebo plus ADT group.
As of the data cutoff on October 14, 2018, median follow-up
time was 14.4 months. Overall, 377 patients (32.8%) dis-
continued study treatment (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 135
[23.5%]; placebo plus ADT, n = 242 [42.0%]). The primary
reason for treatment discontinuation was progressive dis-
ease (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 65 [11.3%] v placebo plus
ADT, n = 171 [29.7%]), followed by patient withdrawal
(n = 25 [4.4%] v n = 30 [5.2%], respectively; Fig 1).
rPFS
At data cutoff, 292 radiographic disease progression events
or deaths without radiographic disease progression within
24 weeks of treatment discontinuation had occurred
(enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 91 [15.9%]; placebo plus
ADT, n = 201 [34.9%]; Table 2). Overall, enzalutamide plus
ADT significantly reduced the risk of radiographic disease
progression or death compared with placebo plus ADT by
61% (HR, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.30 to 0.50; P , .001; Fig 2A).
Median rPFS was not reached (NR) with enzalutamide plus
ADT (95% CI, NR to NR) versus 19.0 months (95% CI, 16.6
to 22.2 months) with placebo plus ADT. The treatment
effect of enzalutamide plus ADT was consistent across all
prespecified subgroups, including disease volume and
prior docetaxel chemotherapy (Fig 2B). A sensitivity
analysis of rPFS, including all deaths (in the absence of
evidence of radiographic disease progression) regardless of
timing, and a sensitivity analysis of radiographic progres-
sion documented by central review according to Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 criteria25 were both consistent
with the primary analysis (Table 2).
Secondary End Points
The superiority of enzalutamide plus ADT over placebo plus
ADT was shown for the key secondary end points of time to
PSA progression, time to initiation of new antineoplastic
therapy, PSA undetectable rate, and objective response
rate (Table 2; Fig 3). Although the median time to initiation
of a new antineoplastic agent of 30.2 months in the
enzalutamide arm is not a reliable estimate because it
resulted from an event observed in the only remaining
patient at risk, the treatment effect was robust, as evi-
denced by the HR of 0.28 (95% CI, 0.20 to 0.40; P , .001).
Of the patients who initiated new antineoplastic therapy, the
most common therapy was abiraterone (n = 13; 28.3%)
followed by docetaxel (n = 11; 23.9%) in the enzalutamide
plus ADT group and docetaxel (n = 52; 39.1%) followed by
abiraterone and enzalutamide (n = 28 each; 21.1%) in the
placebo plus ADT group (Data Supplement Table A3). At
this interim OS analysis, data were immature, with
84 deaths (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 39; placebo plus ADT,
n = 45); median duration of OS was NR in either treatment
group (HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.53 to 1.25; P = .3361; Table 2;
Data Supplement Fig A2). Enzalutamide plus ADT also
significantly reduced the risk of a first symptomatic skeletal

response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

questions.wording: Were participants aware of their assigned intervention during the trial?
questions.official_guidance: If participants are aware of their assigned intervention it is more likely that health-related behaviours will differ between the intervention groups. Blinding participants, most commonly through use of a placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences. If participants experienced side effects or toxicities that they knew to be specific to one of the interventions, answer this question ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether participants were aware of their assigned intervention during the trial.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when participants knew their assignment, including when intervention-specific side effects or toxicities revealed it. Blinding participants, commonly with placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences.
evidence_needed: A direct report of participant blinding, open-label conduct, or participant knowledge during the trial.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an absent explicit awareness statement alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment.

answer_anchors.text: Participants were aware of their assigned intervention.
Participants were blinded to their assigned intervention.

considerations: Awareness is about knowledge of assignment, not whether participants completed or received treatment.

evidence.transcription: Section 4.5, Assign and Allocate: Subjects will be entered into the IRT system at screening and assigned a subject number. Randomization will be performed via the IRT system and treatment assigned in a 1:1 ratio to enzalutamide 160 mg/day or placebo. Before the initiation of study treatment, on day 1, the site staff will contact the IRT system to determine the randomly assigned treatment. Subjects will be stratified by prior docetaxel and disease volume. Specific procedures for randomization through the IRT system are contained in the study procedures manual.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

Radiographic disease progression is defined as

Efficacy analyses were conducted on the intent-to-treat

A two-sided stratified log-rank test at a level of

included QoL over time and sensitivity analyses of time
to pain progression (using other clinically meaningful
threshold criteria). Safety was also assessed. End point
definitions are provided in Data Supplement Table A1.
Assessments
Efficacy assessments included sequential radiographic
imaging performed at screening, at week 13, and every
subsequent 12 weeks. Radiographic progression events
were confirmed by independent central review; details
regarding the definition of radiographic progression, in-
cluding confirmatory scans required for new bone lesions
observed over time, are provided in Data Supplement
Table A2. PSA levels were measured at screening, at weeks
1, 5, and 13, every subsequent 12 weeks, and 30 days after
the last dose or prior to initiation of new antineoplastic
therapy for prostate cancer, whichever occurred first. PRO
assessments, such as Functional Assessment of Cancer
Therapy-Prostate,26 Quality of Life Prostate-Specific
questionnaire 25,27 and Brief Pain Inventory-Short
Form (BPI-SF), were completed at baseline, week 13,
and every 12 weeks thereafter. Adverse events (AEs) were
graded by the investigator according to the National
Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Ad-
verse Events (version 4.03).
Statistical Analysis
The final rPFS analysis was planned to occur after
262 events, to detect a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.67 with 90%
power, on the basis of a two-sided log-rank test and 5%
significance level. To adjust for multiplicity, a parallel testing
strategy was applied to the key secondary end points
(Appendix Fig A1, online only). Key secondary end
points, other than OS, were sequentially tested at a 1%
significance level. A final OS analysis will be performed
when 342 deaths have occurred to provide 80% power to
detect an HR of 0.73 at a 4% significance level. An interim
OS analysis was performed at the time of the final rPFS
analysis at a significance level calculated using the O'Brien-
Fleming function to control the overall alpha. Additional
details regarding the statistical analyses (original and final)
are provided in the Data Supplement (Fig A1 and Table A1)
and Protocol (including SAP).
RESULTS
Patients and Treatment
From March 21, 2016, to January 12, 2018, a total of 1,150
patients were randomly assigned 1:1 from 202 centers in
North and Latin America, Europe, and Asia; 1,146 patients
received at least one dose of the study drug (Fig 1).
Baseline demographics were well balanced between
treatment groups (Table 1); 727 patients (63.2%) had high-
volume disease, and 205 (17.9%) received prior docetaxel
chemotherapy. Use of concomitant antiandrogens as
prostate cancer therapy during the study was reported by
34 patients (5.9%) in the enzalutamide plus ADT group and
43 patients (7.5%) in the placebo plus ADT group.
As of the data cutoff on October 14, 2018, median follow-up
time was 14.4 months. Overall, 377 patients (32.8%) dis-
continued study treatment (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 135
[23.5%]; placebo plus ADT, n = 242 [42.0%]). The primary
reason for treatment discontinuation was progressive dis-
ease (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 65 [11.3%] v placebo plus
ADT, n = 171 [29.7%]), followed by patient withdrawal
(n = 25 [4.4%] v n = 30 [5.2%], respectively; Fig 1).
rPFS
At data cutoff, 292 radiographic disease progression events
or deaths without radiographic disease progression within
24 weeks of treatment discontinuation had occurred
(enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 91 [15.9%]; placebo plus
ADT, n = 201 [34.9%]; Table 2). Overall, enzalutamide plus
ADT significantly reduced the risk of radiographic disease
progression or death compared with placebo plus ADT by
61% (HR, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.30 to 0.50; P , .001; Fig 2A).
Median rPFS was not reached (NR) with enzalutamide plus
ADT (95% CI, NR to NR) versus 19.0 months (95% CI, 16.6
to 22.2 months) with placebo plus ADT. The treatment
effect of enzalutamide plus ADT was consistent across all
prespecified subgroups, including disease volume and
prior docetaxel chemotherapy (Fig 2B). A sensitivity
analysis of rPFS, including all deaths (in the absence of
evidence of radiographic disease progression) regardless of
timing, and a sensitivity analysis of radiographic progres-
sion documented by central review according to Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 criteria25 were both consistent
with the primary analysis (Table 2).
Secondary End Points
The superiority of enzalutamide plus ADT over placebo plus
ADT was shown for the key secondary end points of time to
PSA progression, time to initiation of new antineoplastic
therapy, PSA undetectable rate, and objective response
rate (Table 2; Fig 3). Although the median time to initiation
of a new antineoplastic agent of 30.2 months in the
enzalutamide arm is not a reliable estimate because it
resulted from an event observed in the only remaining
patient at risk, the treatment effect was robust, as evi-
denced by the HR of 0.28 (95% CI, 0.20 to 0.40; P , .001).
Of the patients who initiated new antineoplastic therapy, the
most common therapy was abiraterone (n = 13; 28.3%)
followed by docetaxel (n = 11; 23.9%) in the enzalutamide
plus ADT group and docetaxel (n = 52; 39.1%) followed by
abiraterone and enzalutamide (n = 28 each; 21.1%) in the
placebo plus ADT group (Data Supplement Table A3). At
this interim OS analysis, data were immature, with
84 deaths (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 39; placebo plus ADT,
n = 45); median duration of OS was NR in either treatment
group (HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.53 to 1.25; P = .3361; Table 2;
Data Supplement Fig A2). Enzalutamide plus ADT also
significantly reduced the risk of a first symptomatic skeletal

arguments.transcription: Protocol sections 4.4–4.4.4: This was a double-blind study. Subjects were to receive enzalutamide or placebo such that the investigator, sponsor study-management team, clinical staff, and subject would not know which agent was being administered. The IRT supplied randomization numbers based on information obtained through IRT. Enzalutamide and placebo tablets and their packaging were indistinguishable in appearance. The IRT maintained the randomization list and study-medication blind; the DSMB had access to dosing assignment for periodic review of unblinded data. For a medical emergency, IRT would provide the treatment code; the request and reason had to be documented, and study personnel would not be made aware unless emergency disclosure was necessary. Sponsor code breaks were limited to staff responsible for reporting suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions.

questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.

questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

# Assess missing outcome data

Use this reference for Domain 3. The approved Result fixes the outcome and time
point; the returned question cards fix answer direction and activation.

Every active answer is accompanied by a concise justification, an `unknowns`
array (use `[]` when none are identified), and a `counterevidence` array. A
counterpoint refers to the answer's zero-based basis index, for example:

```json
"counterevidence": [{"basis_index": 0, "implication": "This passage limits the strength of the selected answer."}]
```

Inactive branch answers may be omitted or retained without fabricated reasoning;
the server commits only the dependency-closed active path.

## Availability audit

For D3.1, support Yes or Probably Yes with actual outcome-availability
evidence. Accept one or more of:

- comparable observed-outcome counts for the randomized population;
- arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring rates, reasons, and follow-up
  accounting; or
- an explicit statement that ascertainment was complete or nearly complete.

Support No or Probably No with evidence that availability was materially
incomplete for this Result. If the extent remains unknown after bounded
retrieval, use No information. Failure to demonstrate complete availability is
not evidence that availability was incomplete.

The following do not establish affirmative availability on their own:

- analysis denominators or ITT membership;
- planned or scheduled follow-up;
- treatment continuation or discontinuation; or
- a generic censoring rule without actual rates or follow-up accounting.

For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later
time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not
establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect
outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their
outcome and time window to the approved Result. Recovery may inform bias from
missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

When the availability premise remains unresolved, use the active comparison
card's full Source inventory to inspect unopened supplements or combined
protocol documents. Search for concrete study wording such as the outcome
status, withdrawal or loss-to-follow-up labels, and the reported time point;
`missing outcome data` alone may not occur in the report. Widen the Source
scope or continue a cached cursor only as needed, and stop when comparable
observed counts or complete follow-up accounting are inspected. If the
captured Sources and bounded page windows do not establish availability,
document that limit instead of treating an empty Source group or a no-hit
search as evidence of missing outcomes.

## Reconcile availability

Keep these quantities distinct for each arm and time point:

- randomized participants;
- participants with the outcome observed;
- participants included in the reported analysis;
- participants whose outcomes were imputed; and
- post-randomization exclusions; and
- outcome events, which are a numerator rather than an observed-participant count.

An analyzed count is not necessarily an observed count. Imputed outcomes count
as missing outcome data for RoB 2. Treatment discontinuation is not missing
outcome data when follow-up and outcome ascertainment continued.

If some outcomes are missing, assess whether data remain available for nearly
all randomized participants. Keep the randomized denominator, outcome-observed
count, analyzed count, imputed count, excluded count, and event count separate
for the same arm, population, unit, and time point. Consider whether the
missing outcomes could make an important difference to this Result. For
dichotomous outcomes, compare the missing count with observed events, not only
the randomized denominator. A count below the randomized total does not settle
that question, and no universal percentage threshold replaces this impact
judgment.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring
caused by missing follow-up before the outcome could be observed. Treatment
discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that
outcome observation stopped. For time-to-event Results, censoring may still
create missing outcome information; assess its timing, reason, actual follow-up
pathway, and relation to treatment or prognosis instead of treating every
censored participant as either fully observed or missing by default.

Question 3.1 may include compact `missing_data` rows. Give each row a comparable
arm, population, unit, and time point. Use a row-level `basis` only to narrow or
add to the answer's Evidence. The server calculates differences and fractions
only after scopes match and preserves conflicting reports without choosing the
scientific answer.

When a count comparison would help before answering, call `get_domain_context`
with `missing_data` rows. Every preview row needs a nonempty `basis` containing
current-Trial Evidence references: no answer exists to supply inherited Evidence.
Inspect `comparison_cards[].missing_data`
for differences, fractions, and conflicting reports. The preview changes no
checkpoint or State revision. To retain the chosen rows, submit them with the
3.1 answer in `validate_domain_assessment`; omit row `basis` there only to reuse
the answer's Evidence when it supports those counts. After its receipt, save
the exact draft with `save_domain_judgment`.

Check each input against its source passage before using the arithmetic. The
helper subtracts supplied observed counts from randomized counts; it does not
extract counts or sum grouped departures. Keep unknown observed counts unknown.
Skip the preview when an explicit ascertainment statement resolves availability
without arithmetic.

When a row includes typed `semantics`, treat it as scope metadata, not as a
shortcut to a signalling answer. `event_count` is an event numerator and never
means that every participant's outcome was observed. `analyzed`, `safety`, and
`per_protocol` roles are denominators or populations, not availability. Keep
administrative censoring, loss to follow-up, treatment change, imputation, and
post-randomization exclusions as distinct facts. The server preserves these
fields and only derives `randomized - observed`; it does not decide whether a
censored participant is informative.

## Assess bias from missingness

If data were not available for all or nearly all participants, ask in sequence:

1. Does a bias-correcting method or informative sensitivity analysis show that
   the Result was not biased?
2. Could missingness depend on the true outcome, based on reasons, health
   status, withdrawal, loss to follow-up, or censoring?
3. If it could, is that dependence likely given arm differences, reasons,
   prognostic factors, or trial circumstances?

Simple imputation, including last observation carried forward or multiple
imputation based only on intervention group, does not by itself show freedom from
bias. A comparison that changes group attribution, such as ITT versus
as-treated, does not test unobserved outcome values unless the source establishes
that relationship. A reassuring sensitivity analysis must vary plausible
unobserved outcomes under the missingness mechanism relevant to the approved
Result. Documented reasons support reassurance only when they address the
outcome relationship.

Keep possible dependence in 3.3 separate from likely dependence in 3.4. For
3.4, state which reasons or trial circumstances support the likelihood judgment.
Absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likely dependence. Preserve
`no_information` when the card's uncertainty rule applies, even when that answer
leads to High risk of bias.

D3.2 does not allow `no_information`. When no bias-correcting evidence is found,
use the question card to choose a permitted negative or probably-negative answer
with the appropriate limitation or Evidence basis. Do not fabricate direct
support for the absence of bias.

## Paired premise check

Use neutral pairs to keep the seams separate: complete outcome ascertainment
versus an analysis denominator with unresolved availability; common administrative
censoring versus follow-up stopping after worsening symptoms. The changed premise
is the ascertainment or missingness mechanism, not a percentage threshold. The
pair supplies no answer or risk label; the host still grounds each proposition
in exact Evidence and retains No information or High where the official path
requires it.

This question permits complete ascertainment, mechanism-matched reassurance, and legitimate uncertainty. Do not apply a universal percentage threshold in place of a Result-specific impact judgment.

The assumptions must match the documented missingness mechanism and the approved Result. Last-observation-carried-forward or multiple imputation based only on intervention group should not be assumed to correct bias.

Table A1. End Point Definitions and Analysis Method.
End point variable
Definition and analysis method
Primary
rPFS
Time from randomization to the first objective evidence
of radiographic disease progression as assessed by
central review or death (defined as death from any
cause within 24 weeks from study drug
discontinuation), whichever occurs first
Patients who discontinued study treatment without
confirmed radiographic progression continued the
radiographic assessment schedule until radiographic
progression was confirmed or the number of
radiographic progression events for the final rPFS
analysis was reached
Radiographic disease progression is defined as
progressive disease by RECIST, version 1.1,2 for soft
tissue disease or by appearance of two or more new
lesions on bone scan (see Supplementary Table S2)
Efficacy analyses were conducted on the intent-to-treat
population, defined as all randomized patients
A two-sided stratified log-rank test at a level of
significance of 0.05 was used to compare rPFS between

included QoL over time and sensitivity analyses of time
to pain progression (using other clinically meaningful
threshold criteria). Safety was also assessed. End point
definitions are provided in Data Supplement Table A1.
Assessments
Efficacy assessments included sequential radiographic
imaging performed at screening, at week 13, and every
subsequent 12 weeks. Radiographic progression events
were confirmed by independent central review; details
regarding the definition of radiographic progression, in-
cluding confirmatory scans required for new bone lesions
observed over time, are provided in Data Supplement
Table A2. PSA levels were measured at screening, at weeks
1, 5, and 13, every subsequent 12 weeks, and 30 days after
the last dose or prior to initiation of new antineoplastic
therapy for prostate cancer, whichever occurred first. PRO
assessments, such as Functional Assessment of Cancer
Therapy-Prostate,26 Quality of Life Prostate-Specific
questionnaire 25,27 and Brief Pain Inventory-Short
Form (BPI-SF), were completed at baseline, week 13,
and every 12 weeks thereafter. Adverse events (AEs) were
graded by the investigator according to the National
Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Ad-
verse Events (version 4.03).
Statistical Analysis
The final rPFS analysis was planned to occur after
262 events, to detect a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.67 with 90%
power, on the basis of a two-sided log-rank test and 5%
significance level. To adjust for multiplicity, a parallel testing
strategy was applied to the key secondary end points
(Appendix Fig A1, online only). Key secondary end
points, other than OS, were sequentially tested at a 1%
significance level. A final OS analysis will be performed
when 342 deaths have occurred to provide 80% power to
detect an HR of 0.73 at a 4% significance level. An interim
OS analysis was performed at the time of the final rPFS
analysis at a significance level calculated using the O'Brien-
Fleming function to control the overall alpha. Additional
details regarding the statistical analyses (original and final)
are provided in the Data Supplement (Fig A1 and Table A1)
and Protocol (including SAP).
RESULTS
Patients and Treatment
From March 21, 2016, to January 12, 2018, a total of 1,150
patients were randomly assigned 1:1 from 202 centers in
North and Latin America, Europe, and Asia; 1,146 patients
received at least one dose of the study drug (Fig 1).
Baseline demographics were well balanced between
treatment groups (Table 1); 727 patients (63.2%) had high-
volume disease, and 205 (17.9%) received prior docetaxel
chemotherapy. Use of concomitant antiandrogens as
prostate cancer therapy during the study was reported by
34 patients (5.9%) in the enzalutamide plus ADT group and
43 patients (7.5%) in the placebo plus ADT group.
As of the data cutoff on October 14, 2018, median follow-up
time was 14.4 months. Overall, 377 patients (32.8%) dis-
continued study treatment (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 135
[23.5%]; placebo plus ADT, n = 242 [42.0%]). The primary
reason for treatment discontinuation was progressive dis-
ease (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 65 [11.3%] v placebo plus
ADT, n = 171 [29.7%]), followed by patient withdrawal
(n = 25 [4.4%] v n = 30 [5.2%], respectively; Fig 1).
rPFS
At data cutoff, 292 radiographic disease progression events
or deaths without radiographic disease progression within
24 weeks of treatment discontinuation had occurred
(enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 91 [15.9%]; placebo plus
ADT, n = 201 [34.9%]; Table 2). Overall, enzalutamide plus
ADT significantly reduced the risk of radiographic disease
progression or death compared with placebo plus ADT by
61% (HR, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.30 to 0.50; P , .001; Fig 2A).
Median rPFS was not reached (NR) with enzalutamide plus
ADT (95% CI, NR to NR) versus 19.0 months (95% CI, 16.6
to 22.2 months) with placebo plus ADT. The treatment
effect of enzalutamide plus ADT was consistent across all
prespecified subgroups, including disease volume and
prior docetaxel chemotherapy (Fig 2B). A sensitivity
analysis of rPFS, including all deaths (in the absence of
evidence of radiographic disease progression) regardless of
timing, and a sensitivity analysis of radiographic progres-
sion documented by central review according to Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 criteria25 were both consistent
with the primary analysis (Table 2).
Secondary End Points
The superiority of enzalutamide plus ADT over placebo plus
ADT was shown for the key secondary end points of time to
PSA progression, time to initiation of new antineoplastic
therapy, PSA undetectable rate, and objective response
rate (Table 2; Fig 3). Although the median time to initiation
of a new antineoplastic agent of 30.2 months in the
enzalutamide arm is not a reliable estimate because it
resulted from an event observed in the only remaining
patient at risk, the treatment effect was robust, as evi-
denced by the HR of 0.28 (95% CI, 0.20 to 0.40; P , .001).
Of the patients who initiated new antineoplastic therapy, the
most common therapy was abiraterone (n = 13; 28.3%)
followed by docetaxel (n = 11; 23.9%) in the enzalutamide
plus ADT group and docetaxel (n = 52; 39.1%) followed by
abiraterone and enzalutamide (n = 28 each; 21.1%) in the
placebo plus ADT group (Data Supplement Table A3). At
this interim OS analysis, data were immature, with
84 deaths (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 39; placebo plus ADT,
n = 45); median duration of OS was NR in either treatment
group (HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.53 to 1.25; P = .3361; Table 2;
Data Supplement Fig A2). Enzalutamide plus ADT also
significantly reduced the risk of a first symptomatic skeletal

regarding the definition of radiographic progression, in-
cluding confirmatory scans required for new bone lesions
observed over time, are provided in Data Supplement
Table A2. PSA levels were measured at screening, at weeks
1, 5, and 13, every subsequent 12 weeks, and 30 days after
the last dose or prior to initiation of new antineoplastic
therapy for prostate cancer, whichever occurred first. PRO
assessments, such as Functional Assessment of Cancer
Therapy-Prostate,26 Quality of Life Prostate-Specific
questionnaire 25,27 and Brief Pain Inventory-Short
Form (BPI-SF), were completed at baseline, week 13,
and every 12 weeks thereafter. Adverse events (AEs) were
graded by the investigator according to the National
Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Ad-
verse Events (version 4.03).
Statistical Analysis
The final rPFS analysis was planned to occur after
262 events, to detect a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.67 with 90%
power, on the basis of a two-sided log-rank test and 5%
significance level. To adjust for multiplicity, a parallel testing
strategy was applied to the key secondary end points
(Appendix Fig A1, online only). Key secondary end
points, other than OS, were sequentially tested at a 1%
significance level. A final OS analysis will be performed
when 342 deaths have occurred to provide 80% power to
detect an HR of 0.73 at a 4% significance level. An interim
OS analysis was performed at the time of the final rPFS
analysis at a significance level calculated using the O'Brien-
Fleming function to control the overall alpha. Additional
details regarding the statistical analyses (original and final)
are provided in the Data Supplement (Fig A1 and Table A1)
and Protocol (including SAP).
RESULTS
Patients and Treatment
From March 21, 2016, to January 12, 2018, a total of 1,150
patients were randomly assigned 1:1 from 202 centers in
North and Latin America, Europe, and Asia; 1,146 patients
received at least one dose of the study drug (Fig 1).
Baseline demographics were well balanced between
treatment groups (Table 1); 727 patients (63.2%) had high-
volume disease, and 205 (17.9%) received prior docetaxel
chemotherapy. Use of concomitant antiandrogens as
prostate cancer therapy during the study was reported by
34 patients (5.9%) in the enzalutamide plus ADT group and
43 patients (7.5%) in the placebo plus ADT group.
As of the data cutoff on October 14, 2018, median follow-up
time was 14.4 months. Overall, 377 patients (32.8%) dis-
continued study treatment (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 135
[23.5%]; placebo plus ADT, n = 242 [42.0%]). The primary
reason for treatment discontinuation was progressive dis-
ease (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 65 [11.3%] v placebo plus
ADT, n = 171 [29.7%]), followed by patient withdrawal
(n = 25 [4.4%] v n = 30 [5.2%], respectively; Fig 1).
rPFS
At data cutoff, 292 radiographic disease progression events
or deaths without radiographic disease progression within
24 weeks of treatment discontinuation had occurred
(enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 91 [15.9%]; placebo plus
ADT, n = 201 [34.9%]; Table 2). Overall, enzalutamide plus
ADT significantly reduced the risk of radiographic disease
progression or death compared with placebo plus ADT by
61% (HR, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.30 to 0.50; P , .001; Fig 2A).
Median rPFS was not reached (NR) with enzalutamide plus
ADT (95% CI, NR to NR) versus 19.0 months (95% CI, 16.6
to 22.2 months) with placebo plus ADT. The treatment
effect of enzalutamide plus ADT was consistent across all
prespecified subgroups, including disease volume and
prior docetaxel chemotherapy (Fig 2B). A sensitivity
analysis of rPFS, including all deaths (in the absence of
evidence of radiographic disease progression) regardless of
timing, and a sensitivity analysis of radiographic progres-
sion documented by central review according to Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 criteria25 were both consistent
with the primary analysis (Table 2).
Secondary End Points
The superiority of enzalutamide plus ADT over placebo plus
ADT was shown for the key secondary end points of time to
PSA progression, time to initiation of new antineoplastic
therapy, PSA undetectable rate, and objective response
rate (Table 2; Fig 3). Although the median time to initiation
of a new antineoplastic agent of 30.2 months in the
enzalutamide arm is not a reliable estimate because it
resulted from an event observed in the only remaining
patient at risk, the treatment effect was robust, as evi-
denced by the HR of 0.28 (95% CI, 0.20 to 0.40; P , .001).
Of the patients who initiated new antineoplastic therapy, the
most common therapy was abiraterone (n = 13; 28.3%)
followed by docetaxel (n = 11; 23.9%) in the enzalutamide
plus ADT group and docetaxel (n = 52; 39.1%) followed by
abiraterone and enzalutamide (n = 28 each; 21.1%) in the
placebo plus ADT group (Data Supplement Table A3). At
this interim OS analysis, data were immature, with
84 deaths (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 39; placebo plus ADT,
n = 45); median duration of OS was NR in either treatment
group (HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.53 to 1.25; P = .3361; Table 2;
Data Supplement Fig A2). Enzalutamide plus ADT also
significantly reduced the risk of a first symptomatic skeletal

evidence.transcription: Protocol sections 4.4–4.4.4: This was a double-blind study. Subjects were to receive enzalutamide or placebo such that the investigator, sponsor study-management team, clinical staff, and subject would not know which agent was being administered. The IRT supplied randomization numbers based on information obtained through IRT. Enzalutamide and placebo tablets and their packaging were indistinguishable in appearance. The IRT maintained the randomization list and study-medication blind; the DSMB had access to dosing assignment for periodic review of unblinded data. For a medical emergency, IRT would provide the treatment code; the request and reason had to be documented, and study personnel would not be made aware unless emergency disclosure was necessary. Sponsor code breaks were limited to staff responsible for reporting suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions.

Section 4.5, Assign and Allocate: Subjects will be entered into the IRT system at screening and assigned a subject number. Randomization will be performed via the IRT system and treatment assigned in a 1:1 ratio to enzalutamide 160 mg/day or placebo. Before the initiation of study treatment, on day 1, the site staff will contact the IRT system to determine the randomly assigned treatment. Subjects will be stratified by prior docetaxel and disease volume. Specific procedures for randomization through the IRT system are contained in the study procedures manual.
